title: SR&ED Eligible Materials in the R&D Process | Canada FAQ
description: Are materials used in the R&D process eligible for the SR&ED tax credit in Canada? Check our FAQ on qualifying materials consumed or transformed.
summary: In Canada, eligible SR&ED materials are those consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, available to claimants under either the proxy or traditional method. Costs are claimed only in the taxation year the materials are consumed or transformed, and transformed materials later sold or converted to commercial use can trigger investment tax credit recapture.

Costs are claimed only in the taxation year the materials are consumed or transformed, and transformed materials later sold or converted to commercial use can trigger investment tax credit recapture.

Canada's flagship R&D tax incentive, the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Program, operates through a dual-mechanism statutory architecture under the federal Income Tax Act (ITA): first, an immediate 100% income tax deduction (or indefinite pool carryforward) for allowable current and capital SR&ED expenditures under section 37; and second, a volume-based Investment Tax Credit (ITC) on qualified SR&ED expenditures under sections 127 and 127.1. Following the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, and applies retroactively to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the federal SR&ED landscape underwent its largest structural expansion in over a decade:

items: Doubling of the Enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit: The maximum annual expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% federal ITC doubled from $3 million to $6 million, increasing the maximum annual refundable federal cash credit on current expenditures from $1.05 million to $2.1 million.

Expansion of Taxable Capital Phase-Out Thresholds: For Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs), the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada phase-out range expanded from the historical $10 million–$50 million corridor to a substantially wider $15 million–$75 million corridor.

Extension of Enhanced 35% Refundable Credits to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and Revenue Phase-Out Election: Bill C-15 created a new statutory category—the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—granting qualifying Canadian-resident public companies access to the 35% refundable ITC on up to $6 million of expenditures, phased out over three-year average annual gross revenue between $15 million and $75 million. Furthermore, CCPCs may now elect annually under subsection 127(10.31) to calculate their expenditure limit phase-out using the $15 million–$75 million three-year average gross revenue test rather than taxable capital.

Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Equipment Leases: Reversing the post-2013 exclusion, Bill C-15 restored SR&ED deductibility under paragraph 37(1)(b) and ITC eligibility under subsection 127(9) for depreciable capital property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (including Shared-Use Equipment [SUE] used primarily for SR&ED), as well as qualifying equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024.

Introduction of Optional Pre-Claim Approval (Form T1322): On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched a voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process using Form T1322 for businesses with gross business income under $25 million, providing formal upfront technical eligibility determinations within 8 weeks and accelerating post-filing refund processing to 90 days.

body.text: At the provincial level, Québec simultaneously executed a landmark overhaul of its innovation tax system for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing legacy R&D tax measures with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1 million of eligible R&D, pre-commercialization, and capital equipment spending above an exclusion threshold, and 20% thereafter. Similarly, British Columbia aligned its 10% provincial SR&ED tax credit in its February 17, 2026 budget with the federal Bill C-15 capital restoration, $6 million expenditure limit, and $15 million–$75 million phase-out thresholds.
1. Statutory and Regulatory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Historical Evolution and Governing Authorities

Canada's statutory encouragement of industrial research traces its legislative lineage to 1944 amendments to the Income War Tax Act, which first permitted Canadian corporations to deduct research and development outlays that would otherwise be disallowed on account of capital under the general limitation rules now codified in section 18 of the Income Tax Act. The modern two-tiered incentive structure—combining an expenditure deduction pool with an investment tax credit—has operated under the SR&ED banner since 1986. According to CRA program statistics cited in industry analyses, in the 2024–2025 fiscal period the CRA processed 22,758 SR&ED claims and approved $4.5 billion in investment tax credits across Canada, with small businesses accounting for 65% of all submitted claims in the 2025–2026 fiscal cycle.

The federal SR&ED program is co-governed by two federal institutions. The Department of Finance Canada is responsible for drafting legislative policy, statutory amendments to the Income Tax Act, and regulatory prescriptions under the Income Tax Regulations. The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is responsible for the daily administration of the program, promulgating administrative policies and technical guidelines, conducting technical reviews through Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) and financial audits through Financial Reviewers (FRs), administering the Pre-Claim Approval Process and First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), and assessing income tax returns.

The core statutory and regulatory provisions governing the federal SR&ED regime are distributed across five primary instruments in the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations. First, subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act contains the foundational legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" (paragraphs (a) through (k)), alongside essential definitions for "salary or wages", "property", and "disposition". Second, section 37 of the Income Tax Act governs the calculation, additions, reductions, and optional deduction of the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures carried on in Canada (subsection 37(1)) and outside Canada (subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2)), the available-for-use timing rule for capital property (subsection 37(1.2)), the prohibition on deducting payments for acquiring rights in or arising out of SR&ED (subsection 37(4)), loss restriction event rules (subsection 37(6.1)), traditional and proxy expenditure definitions (subsection 37(8)), specified employee bonus exclusions (subsection 37(9)), the irrevocable proxy method election (subsection 37(10)), and the strict 18-month reporting deadline (subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12)).

Third, section 127 of the Income Tax Act governs the computation and application of the basic 15% SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (paragraph (a.1) of the definition "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), and subsection 127(5)), partnership allocations (subsection 127(8)), definitions of "investment tax credit", "qualified expenditure", "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool", "contract payment", "government assistance", "non-government assistance", "taxable supplier", "first term shared-use-equipment", "second term shared-use-equipment", "eligible Canadian public corporation", and "eligible subsidiary" (subsection 127(9)), the enhanced 20% top-up credit creating the 35% enhanced rate (subsection 127(10.1)), expenditure limit calculations and phase-outs for CCPCs and ECPCs (subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.64)), capital acquisition timing (subsection 127(11.2)), non-arm's length cost adjustments and transfers (subsections 127(11.5) to 127(11.8), 127(13), and 127(24)), assistance reductions and allocations (subsections 127(18) to 127(20)), unpaid amounts (subsection 127(26)), and ITC recapture mechanics (subsections 127(27) to 127(36)).

Fourth, section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act establishes the refundability mechanism for unused SR&ED ITCs, defining "refundable investment tax credit", "qualifying corporation", and "excluded corporation" (subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01)), and deeming refunded credits to have been deducted against Part I tax payable (subsection 127.1(3)). Fifth, Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Sections 2900–2903) prescribes the expenditures directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED and the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment under the traditional method (Regulations 2900(2) and 2900(3)), the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) formula (Regulation 2900(4)), the specified employee proxy salary base limits and exclusions (Regulations 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9)), the definition of Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) excluded from Shared-Use Equipment (Regulation 2900(11)), prescribed non-qualifying expenditures (Regulation 2902), and prescribed special-purpose buildings (Regulation 2903).
1.2 The Statutory Definition of SR&ED (Subsection 248(1))

To qualify for any tax relief under sections 37, 127, or 127.1, the underlying technical activities must satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, which conforms broadly to the OECD Frascati Manual. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED through a mandatory preamble, three core categories of research, one conditional category of support work, and seven explicit exclusions.
The Preamble

Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Every word in this preamble carries legal weight: the work cannot be a random or trial-and-error exercise, must occur within a recognized branch of natural or applied science or technology (excluding social sciences and humanities), and must proceed specifically by way of physical or empirical experimentation or rigorous mathematical and engineering analysis.
Primary Research Categories: Paragraphs (a), (b), and (c)

The systematic investigation or search must be undertaken for one of three primary statutory purposes. Under paragraph (a) (Basic Research), eligible work is undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. While historically associated with universities and research institutes, basic research is also conducted by commercial enterprises in sectors such as biotechnology, nanotechnology, and advanced materials science. Under paragraph (b) (Applied Research), eligible work is undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view, seeking to expand the underlying scientific knowledge base in order to solve a targeted practical or industrial problem.

Under paragraph (c) (Experimental Development), eligible work is undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development represents the overwhelming majority of industrial SR&ED claims in Canada. Crucially, the statute explicitly protects incremental technological improvements: a claimant does not need to invent a radical, disruptive, or world-first product category, provided the incremental improvement requires overcoming a genuine technological uncertainty to advance the underlying technology base.
Conditional Support Work: Paragraph (d)

Under paragraph (d) of the definition in subsection 248(1), work does not constitute SR&ED in isolation, but qualifies as part of an SR&ED project if and only if it is directly in support of, and commensurate with the needs of, basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c). Paragraph (d) restricts eligible support work to an exhaustive list of eight statutory categories:

items: Engineering;
Design;
Operations research;
Mathematical analysis;
Computer programming;
Data collection;
Testing; and
Psychological research.

body.text: If a claimant performs computer programming, CAD design, or laboratory testing for routine commercial purposes, it is ineligible; however, to the extent those exact activities are required to build test harnesses, fabricate experimental jigs, collect experimental metrics, or validate a hypothesis aimed at resolving a scientific or technological uncertainty, they are fully eligible under paragraph (d).
Statutory Exclusions: Paragraphs (e) to (k)
Subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes work with respect to specific commercial, routine, or non-scientific activities grouped under paragraphs (e) through (k):

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;
Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas;
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes; and
Paragraph (k): Routine data collection.

body.text: As emphasized in the CRA's Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentives (dated August 13, 2021), the distinguishing factor between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as "data collection" or "testing") and excluded work under paragraphs (f) and (k) ("routine testing" or "routine data collection") is purpose. When data collection or testing is carried out specifically to test a hypothesis and resolve a technological uncertainty within an SR&ED investigation, it qualifies under paragraph (d); when conducted for regulatory compliance, quality assurance, or standard commercial operation, it is barred by paragraphs (f) and (k). Similarly, while prospecting or drilling for minerals or petroleum is excluded under paragraph (h), conducting eligible SR&ED concurrently with mineral exploration remains claimable provided the prospecting activities themselves are excluded from the claim.
1.3 CRA's Two-Pillar Eligibility Methodology: The "Why" and "How" Requirements

In administering subsection 248(1), the CRA's August 13, 2021 Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives synthesize the statutory text and Tax Court jurisprudence into two mandatory, cumulative pillars: the "Why" requirement (purpose) and the "How" requirement (manner).
Pillar 1: The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement)

Work must be undertaken for the purpose of achieving scientific or technological advancement. The CRA distinguishes between factual knowledge (measurements, observations, or performance characteristics of known materials or systems) and conceptual knowledge (explanatory theories, predictive models, or principles of how and why a technology behaves under specific conditions). An SR&ED project must seek to generate or discover new conceptual knowledge.

The need for new conceptual knowledge arises only when the claimant encounters a scientific or technological uncertainty—defined as a limitation or insufficiency in the combined scientific or technological knowledge base reasonably available to the business (comprising both the company's internal technical expertise and publicly accessible literature, patents, vendor documentation, and industry standards) that prevents a competent professional in the field from predicting whether a given objective or design can be achieved, or how to achieve it.

According to the CRA's guidelines and Tax Court jurisprudence, technological insufficiency in experimental development typically manifests through several recognizable patterns. First, system uncertainty arises even when individual components, algorithms, or materials are known, if integrating them into a complex system creates unpredictable interactions, feedback loops, or conflicting physical or computational behaviours that cannot be resolved using standard engineering principles. Second, interlocking constraints occur when pushing one performance parameter (such as miniaturization or strength) degrades another critical parameter (such as thermal dissipation, battery life, or weight) beyond the boundaries of known design equations. Cost or economic constraints are not technological uncertainties in themselves, but they can create a technological uncertainty if achieving required technical specifications within a target material or architectural constraint is beyond available technological knowledge. Third, technological insufficiency is indicated when existing design methods are not applicable, specifications do not conform to existing standards, parameters lie outside normal operating ranges, too many variables or unknowns interact simultaneously, or required data is not readily available.

Crucially, commercial or technical success is irrelevant to satisfying the "Why" requirement. As Justice Bowman established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) and affirmed in Rainbow Pipe Line Co. v. The Queen (99 DTC 1081), the rejection of a hypothesis after rigorous testing is itself a technological advancement because it eliminates a previously untested path and expands the technological knowledge base. Conversely, if a company encounters a technical problem and simply circumvents it with a workaround using available knowledge, or acquires already-existing knowledge by hiring an outside expert, training staff, or purchasing proprietary knowledge, no technological advancement is sought and the work is ineligible.
Pillar 2: The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

Merely encountering a difficult technical problem is insufficient; the claimant must address the uncertainty through a systematic investigation or search carried out by means of experiment or analysis. Under the CRA guidelines and the five-step Northwest Hydraulic framework, a systematic investigation requires four sequential operational steps:

items: Defining the Problem and Formulating a Hypothesis: Identifying the specific scientific or technological uncertainty and generating a testable idea, proposed solution, method, or approach consistent with known facts to serve as a starting point toward resolving that uncertainty.

Planning and Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Designing and executing structured physical experiments, prototypes, or mathematical and computational analyses specifically aimed at testing the hypothesis, where the idea or hypothesis can evolve and change as a result of testing.

Developing Logical Conclusions: Evaluating the empirical or analytical results or findings against the hypothesis to formulate logical conclusions and iteratively modify the hypothesis for subsequent testing cycles.
Maintaining Contemporaneous Evidence: Keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses to substantiate the hypotheses tested, experiments conducted, and conclusions reached.

body.text: 1.4 Special Operational Contexts: Production Runs, Prototypes, Pilot Plants, and Custom Assets

When experimental development takes place outside a dedicated laboratory—such as on a commercial factory shop floor or during the construction of a custom commercial machine—special segregation rules apply under the CRA's SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (updated July 19, 2016) and SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (updated July 19, 2016).

When experimental development is performed during a production run, the context is classified as either Experimental Development resulting in Experimental Production (ED+EP) or Experimental Development concurrent with Commercial Production (ED+CP). Output is classified as Experimental Production (ED+EP) when the purpose of the production run is specifically to evaluate the technical aspects of the SR&ED project. Any output produced beyond what is required for the SR&ED evaluation is classified as excess production (or commercial production) and is excluded under paragraph 248(1)(i). When SR&ED occurs simultaneously with commercial production (such as agricultural or industrial trials alongside commercial batches), only the additional (incremental) costs incurred for materials or operations attributable to SR&ED can be claimed, while costs that would have been incurred in normal commercial production are excluded.

A prototype is defined by the CRA as a trial model or preliminary version developed to test the feasibility of a concept or hypothesis within a systematic investigation or search, generally having no lasting value. If duplicate copies of a prototype are constructed for testing prior to commercial production, they may qualify as materials for SR&ED if the testing is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of SR&ED; however, the expenditures are claimed as materials consumed or transformed in the taxation year in which testing is completed, not when the copies are constructed. Receiving payment for tested prototype copies does not alter their nature as materials transformed if commercial production has not started, though it triggers ITC recapture upon disposition. Conversely, building copies to meet market demand or establish inventory after successful testing constitutes excluded commercial production.

A pilot plant is a non-commercial-scale production facility developed for the primary purpose of carrying out SR&ED during its useful life, used solely for technical and experimental content, and isolated from normal business operations. If a plant is developed for temporary or permanent conversion to commercial operations during or after SR&ED work, it does not meet the definition of a pilot plant. Production resulting from a pilot plant is considered experimental production and cannot be used for commercial production, sales promotion, or technology demonstration. In a commercial plant (a facility used for commercial or non-SR&ED production), claimants must strictly separate SR&ED work from non-SR&ED work, and only the segregated labour, materials consumed, and materials transformed to resolve technological uncertainties of the plant or its incorporated equipment qualify.

Finally, a custom product is an asset developed for the purpose of subsequently being sold to meet customer specifications or market-driven technical requirements, whereas a commercial asset is developed for internal use within the company's own business operations. The CRA strictly prohibits the practice of claiming all costs of materials transformed in a custom product or commercial asset upfront and relying on ITC recapture rules in the year of disposition or conversion to commercial use. Instead, only the labour, contracts, and materials consumed or transformed in the specific components undergoing SR&ED work are allowable. In exceptional cases where it is impossible for both the claimant and the CRA to isolate the SR&ED work from the commercial construction of a custom product or commercial asset, the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy permits an Alternative Approach—conditional upon the CRA agreeing to its use and the claimant signing a binding legal waiver of the right to object or appeal under subsection 169(2.2) of the Income Tax Act—calculated using the formula:
Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures = (Total Project Costs Incurred − Estimated Cost of Asset if Technology Had Already Existed) + Estimated Cost of Materials Transformed in SR&ED
2. Federal SR&ED Tax Incentives: Section 37 Pool, Section 127 ITC Rates, and Bill C-15 Phase-Out Mechanics

Calculating a federal SR&ED claim requires two distinct statutory computations: first, determining the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under section 37; and second, determining Qualified SR&ED Expenditures to compute the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) under sections 127 and 127.1. An expenditure may be 100% deductible under section 37 without generating an equivalent qualified expenditure under section 127 (for example, non-arm's length contract payments, used capital equipment, or the 20% excluded portion of arm's length contracts), and conversely, the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) additions generate an ITC under section 127 without ever entering the section 37 deduction pool.
2.1 The Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures

Rather than deducting R&D costs under general business income rules in section 9 (or depreciating them via Capital Cost Allowance [CCA] under paragraph 20(1)(a)), subsection 37(1) aggregates all allowable SR&ED expenditures into a cumulative tax account known as the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (tracked in Part 3, Section C of Form T661, Lines 420 to 470).
Additions to the Section 37 Pool (Subsection 37(1))

Under the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy (updated March 30, 2022) and the Bill C-15 legislative amendments, the pool balance is increased each taxation year by seven statutory components:

items: Allowable Current SR&ED Expenditures in Canada (Paragraph 37(1)(a)): Including eligible salaries and wages of employees (plus permissible foreign SR&ED wages up to the 10% cap under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)), materials consumed or transformed, equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, SR&ED contracts performed on the claimant's behalf (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), third-party payments (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and (ii)), and actual directly related and incremental overhead expenditures if the Traditional Method is elected.

Allowable Capital SR&ED Expenditures in Canada (Paragraph 37(1)(b)): Depreciable property (excluding buildings and leasehold interests in buildings) acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, intended to be used all or substantially all (≥90%) in SR&ED in Canada over its expected useful life or have ≥90% of its value consumed in SR&ED in Canada.
Prior Year's Undeducted Pool Balance (Line 450): Carried forward from the end of the preceding taxation year.
Repayments of Assistance (Line 445): Amounts of government or non-government assistance repaid by the claimant in the year that had previously reduced the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d).

Negative Pool Income Inclusions (Paragraph 12(1)(v)): Any negative Section 37 pool balance that was required to be included in the claimant's taxable income in a previous taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v), restoring the opening pool balance to nil.
Recaptured SR&ED ITCs from the Prior Year (Line 453): Any SR&ED ITC recapture amount added to Part I tax payable in the preceding taxation year under subsections 127(27) to 127(35).

Amalgamation or Wind-Up Transfers (Line 452): Undeducted Section 37 pool balances inherited from a predecessor corporation upon a qualifying amalgamation (paragraph 87(2)(l)) or winding-up (paragraph 88(1)(e.2)).

body.text: Reductions to the Section 37 Pool and Paragraph 12(1)(v) Income Inclusion
The Section 37 pool is reduced each taxation year by five statutory items:

items: Government and Non-Government Assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(d)): All government assistance (including provincial R&D tax credits and grants) and non-government assistance that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED expenditures claimed in the pool. Assistance attributable to the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount does not reduce the Section 37 pool because the PPA is not in the pool; instead, such assistance is included directly in business income in the tax year received.
Provincial Super-Allowance Benefit Amounts: Any "super-allowance benefit amount" for the year or preceding taxation years in respect of a province.

Prior-Year Federal SR&ED ITCs Applied or Refunded (Paragraph 37(1)(e), Line 435): Any federal SR&ED ITC claimed in a preceding taxation year—whether applied to reduce Part I tax payable, carried back to prior years, or received as a cash refund—reduces the current year's Section 37 pool. This mechanism provides a one-year deferral before the federal ITC is taxed: if a claimant has a zero pool balance in the subsequent year because it deducted its entire Section 37 pool in Year 1, the Year 2 reduction for the Year 1 ITC creates a negative Section 37 pool balance at the end of Year 2, which must be brought into net income for tax purposes in Year 2 under paragraph 12(1)(v).
Sale of SR&ED Capital Assets and Other Deductions (Line 440): Dispositions of SR&ED capital assets, CCA recapture, and amounts deducted with respect to insolvency in preceding years.

Optional Current-Year Deduction (Line 460): For corporations, individuals, and trusts, deducting from the Section 37 pool is optional: the taxpayer may deduct any amount up to the current year's amount available for deduction (Line 455) to reduce net income for tax purposes (reported on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), and carry forward the remaining pool balance (Line 470) indefinitely to future taxation years. By contrast, a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance and must deduct 100% of its pool in calculating partnership net income in the year incurred.

body.text: Statutory Prohibition on Acquiring Rights (Subsection 37(4)) and Loss Restriction Events (Subsection 37(6.1))

Under subsection 37(4) of the Income Tax Act, no deduction under section 37 (and no ITC under section 127) is permitted for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (such as purchasing a patent, software copyright, or technology licence developed by another party). This restriction applies regardless of whether SR&ED expenditures were ever claimed for that work in the past or whether the work was performed by a non-resident entity, ensuring that only the performer (or payer on whose behalf the SR&ED was performed in Canada) receives the tax incentive.

Under subsection 37(6.1), if a corporation or trust undergoes a loss restriction event (such as an acquisition of control of a corporation or a new majority-interest beneficiary of a trust), a deemed taxation year-end is triggered immediately prior to the event, and the entity's Section 37 pool is reduced to nil. In subsequent taxation years following the loss restriction event, the undeducted pre-acquisition Section 37 pool balance may be reinstated, carried forward, and deducted only if the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditure related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and only to the extent of the entity's income for the taxation year (before making any Section 37 deduction) derived from that same business or a similar business.
2.2 Federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Rates, Refundability, and Carryover Rules

Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), 127(10.1), and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, as detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 7, 2026), federal SR&ED ITCs are earned as a percentage of the taxpayer's SR&ED Qualified Expenditure Pool at the end of the taxation year (after subtracting any provincial super-allowance benefit amounts). No ITC may be earned on an SR&ED expenditure incurred in the course of earning income if any of the claimant's income is exempt from Part I tax (such as Crown-owned corporations, other than Prescribed Federal Crown Corporations).
The Two Rate Tiers: 35% Enhanced Rate vs. 15% Basic Rate

The Enhanced 35% ITC Rate (under subsection 127(10.1), comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% enhancement) is earned by qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) (as defined in subsection 125(7)) and, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) (as defined in subsection 127(9)), on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual Expenditure Limit ($6 million for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; $3 million for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024).

The Basic 15% ITC Rate (under subsection 127(9), reduced from 20% after 2013) applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, and other non-CCPC/non-ECPC corporate entities on 100% of their qualified expenditures. It also applies to qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs on the portion of their annual qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their available Expenditure Limit, as well as to individuals (sole proprietors), beneficiaries of trusts, and members of partnerships. Because subsection 127(8) computes partnership ITCs at the partnership level where the 20% CCPC enhancement under subsection 127(10.1) is unavailable, partnerships earn only the 15% basic rate even if all partners are CCPCs, as confirmed in All Colour Chemicals.
Refundability Matrix (Section 127.1)

Whether an unused SR&ED ITC (after offsetting all federal Part I income tax otherwise payable in the current year under subsection 127(5)) is refunded in cash by the CRA under section 127.1 depends on the claimant's entity classification and whether the expenditure is current or capital:

items: CCPCs and ECPCs Within the $6 Million Expenditure Limit: For current expenditures, the 35% enhanced ITC is 100% refundable in cash (yielding a 35% cash recovery on qualified current spending). Following the elimination of the federal taxable income phase-out threshold for taxation years ending after March 18, 2019, this 100% cash refund on current costs within the expenditure limit does not depend on prior-year taxable income, applying to any eligible CCPC (other than an "excluded corporation" under subsection 127.1(2)). For capital expenditures (depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024), the 35% enhanced ITC is 40% refundable in cash (yielding a 14% immediate cash refund and a 21% non-refundable credit available for carryover).

CCPCs and ECPCs Above the Expenditure Limit: Qualified expenditures exceeding the annual expenditure limit earn the 15% basic ITC rate; this 15% credit is generally non-refundable (0% refund), though a CCPC that meets the specific definition of a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) may access a 40% refund rate on current expenditures.
Individuals (Sole Proprietors), Certain Trusts, and Unincorporated Businesses: Earn the 15% basic ITC rate (claimed on Form T2038(IND)), which is 40% refundable in cash (yielding a 6% cash refund).
Other Corporations (Foreign-Controlled Subsidiaries, Non-ECPC Public Corporations): Earn the 15% basic ITC rate, which is 0% refundable (100% non-refundable).

body.text: Carryback, Carryforward, and Loss Restriction Event Rules

Any portion of an SR&ED ITC that is not applied against current-year Part I tax payable and is not refunded under section 127.1 may be carried back up to 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to offset Part I tax payable. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash in the taxation year is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable in that year, reducing the ITC balance available for carryforward or carryback and triggering the subsequent year's Section 37 pool reduction. As the Tax Court confirmed in Ainsworth Lumber Co. v. The Queen (98-1052-IT-G, 2001), because subsection 127(5) provides that a taxpayer "may" deduct credits, a taxpayer may elect the order in which it utilizes credits. Finally, an acquisition of control (loss restriction event) restricts the carryforward of unused ITCs earned prior to the acquisition and restricts the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition.
2.3 Bill C-15 Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas ($6M Limit, $15M–$75M Grind)

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, Royal Assent March 26, 2026) fundamentally modernized the expenditure limit and phase-out formulas under subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.64) of the Income Tax Act.
1. CCPC Standard Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

For a stand-alone CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs allocating the limit on Schedule T2SCH49 under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3)), the base annual Expenditure Limit is $6,000,000 (up from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). This $6 million limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the corporation's (or associated group's combined) taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under section 181.2, 181.3, or 181.4 for the immediately preceding taxation year, which generally includes retained earnings, contributed surplus, and indebtedness, minus investments and loans to other corporations) reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated at $75,000,000:
Expenditure Limit<sub>CCPC (Capital)</sub> = $6,000,000 × [$60,000,000 − max($0, min($60,000,000, Taxable Capital − $15,000,000))] ÷ $60,000,000

Equivalently, for prior-year taxable capital between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, every $10 of taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $1. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the formula used a $3,000,000 base limit and phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital.
2. Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) and Electing CCPC Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula (Subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.62))

Bill C-15 introduced the Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) and "eligible subsidiary" definitions in subsection 127(9), granting Canadian-resident public corporations (and their eligible subsidiaries) access to the 35% refundable ITC. For an ECPC (or a consolidated group of ECPCs under subsection 127(10.62)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is phased out based exclusively on its average annual gross revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years. Under the CRA's SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, calculating the 3-year average annual revenue requires using the total of all amounts of average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements (or consolidated financial statements as defined in subsection 233.8(1)) for each corporation that is a member of the group for the taxation year in question over the preceding 3 fiscal years—regardless of whether the corporations were associated during the entirety of that period—with reasonable adjustments permitted for intra-group sales of goods or services so that group revenue reflects a single economic entity.

The full $6,000,000 expenditure limit applies when 3-year average annual gross revenue (Ravg) is $15,000,000 or less, decreases linearly between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, and reaches $0 at $75,000,000:

Crucially, under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs where all CCPCs in the group jointly elect and allocate the limit on prescribed forms) may elect annually to have its $6,000,000 expenditure limit determined using this exact 3-year average gross revenue phase-out formula rather than the prior-year taxable capital formula. This provides a major planning avenue for capital-intensive CCPCs (such as biotechnology, clean-tech hardware, or advanced manufacturing firms) that have accumulated debt or share capital exceeding $15 million in taxable capital while generating under $15 million in gross revenue.
3. Short Taxation Years and Associated Corporation De-Association Relief

If a corporation's taxation year is shorter than 51 weeks (for example, due to incorporation, change of year-end, amalgamation, or an acquisition of control), its annual expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365:
Prorated Expenditure Limit = Expenditure Limit × (Number of Days in Taxation Year ÷ 365)

Specific statutory rules also govern expenditure limit determinations when a CCPC or ECPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated with another CCPC (or is a member of a consolidated ECPC group) in two or more of those taxation years.

Furthermore, under the general corporate association rules in section 256, if two otherwise unassociated corporations are associated with the same third corporation, they are deemed associated with each other, and CCPCs can also be considered associated when the same group of otherwise unconnected investors (such as venture capital funds) owns shares in each of them. To prevent the receipt of SR&ED tax incentives by small businesses from being hindered in venture capital investment scenarios, the Income Tax Act provides specific relieving provisions deeming corporations not to be associated for purposes of calculating the expenditure limit and refundable ITC if the sole reason one corporation is associated with another is that two or more investors own shares in each corporation, provided that at least one shareholder of one of the corporations is not a shareholder of the other corporation, and the existence of that distinct shareholder is not for the purpose of satisfying these relieving provisions. Conversely, in assessing de facto control under subsection 256(5.1) (which can strip CCPC status if a public or foreign entity exercises control in fact), the courts examine operational influence and board control, as established in HSC Research (1995 TCC), Mimetex Pharmaceutical (1999 TCC), McGillivray Restaurant Ltd. v. The Queen (2016 FCA), Mindready Solutions (2015 TCC 17), Aeronautic Development Corp. (2017 TCC 39), and CO2 Solution Technologies (2019 TCC 286).

body.text: 3. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methods, and Capital Property Rules

To compute a claim on Form T661, a taxpayer must first determine its Allowable SR&ED Expenditures in Part 3 (Lines 300–400) and then adjust those figures in Part 4 (Lines 500–570) to arrive at Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for ITC purposes under subsection 127(9) and the CRA's Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy (updated May 22, 2026).
3.1 Salaries and Wages (Domestic, Specified Employees, 180-Day Rule, and 10% Foreign Limit)

Salaries and wages typically form the largest component of Canadian SR&ED claims and are governed by subsection 248(1), subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), 37(8), 37(9), 78(4), Regulations 2900(7)–(9), and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025).
1. Statutory Scope of "Salary or Wages"

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, "salary or wages" means the income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (Sections 5 to 8—that is, T4 employment remuneration). Consequently, dividends paid to shareholder-founders, management fees billed by a corporation, retiring allowances (except when directly related and incremental as overhead under the Traditional Method), the value of non-cash taxable benefits, and employee stock option benefits (disallowed for SR&ED after November 14, 2005, overturning Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149) cannot be claimed as SR&ED salary or wages. Furthermore, under subsection 248(16), any GST/HST or PST component included on an employee's T4 slip for a taxable benefit for which the employer claims an input tax credit is deemed to be government assistance and must be excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages.
2. "Directly Engaged" Employees vs. Other Technical Support/Supervisory Staff

Whether an employee's salary is claimable depends on the tasks performed—not the employee's job title—and on whether the claimant elects the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Under the Proxy Method, only salary or wages for employees directly engaged in SR&ED may be claimed and included in the salary base. "Directly engaged in SR&ED" refers to hands-on technical work, including conducting experiments or analyses, performing eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work, performing non-specialized tasks (such as operating a machine or feeding raw materials during an experimental trial) under the direct supervision of technical staff, direct first-line technical supervision of SR&ED personnel and technical contract administration, technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects (such as assignment of technological personnel, job priorities, development of technological strategies, and quality of materials used), feasibility studies, and preparing internal technical documentation.

If an employee devotes all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of their working time to SR&ED, all of their eligible salary is considered related to SR&ED; otherwise, the directly engaged salary is prorated based on the time spent directly engaged in SR&ED relative to total hours worked (for example, 1,800 SR&ED hours divided by 2,400 total hours worked equals 75% of salary). Extended vacation or extended sick leave amounts are considered not directly engaged. Salaries of administrative, clerical, or general support employees who are not directly engaged cannot be claimed under the Proxy Method because those amounts are captured by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. Under the Traditional Method, by contrast, claimants claim both directly engaged salaries and the salaries of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the performance of SR&ED (other than directly engaged), as well as administrative or clerical salaries that are directly attributable (directly related and incremental) as overhead and other expenditures on Line 360.
3. Specified Employee Restrictions (Shareholder-Employees)

A specified employee is an employee who is a specified shareholder of the employer corporation (owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of any related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. Because specified employees can influence their own compensation structures, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose strict exclusions and dual-layer caps on their remuneration (reported on Line 305 for Canadian work, Line 309 for foreign work, and Part 5 Section A, Boxes 850–860 for the Proxy Salary Base).

First, under subsection 37(9) and Regulation 2900(9), for a specified employee, all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310) are strictly excluded from both allowable SR&ED expenditures (Part 3) and the Proxy Salary Base (Part 5). By contrast, bonuses and profit-based remuneration paid to non-specified employees can be included in Part 3 allowable SR&ED expenditures if reasonably linked to SR&ED, though they must be subtracted on Line 812 when computing the Part 5 Proxy Salary Base.

Second, in Part 3 (Allowable SR&ED Expenditures), the maximum amount of salary or wages claimable for a specified employee (Lines 305 and 309) is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the employee is a specified employee:
Maximum Part 3 Specified Employee Salary = 5 × YMPE × (Days as Specified Employee in Tax Year ÷ 365)

If a specified employee also performs SR&ED work for one or more associated corporations, this maximum allowable salary cap must be allocated among the associated corporations using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) under subsection 37(9.3).

Third, in Part 5 (Proxy Salary Base, Boxes 850 to 860), under Regulations 2900(7) and 2900(8), the amount that a claimant can include in the salary base for a specified employee to earn the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (entered in Box 860 and carried to Line 816, which cannot exceed the total of Lines 305 and 309) is restricted to the lesser of two amounts:

items: Box 856 (The 75% Cap): 100% of the specified employee's total base salary or wages for the year (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, profit-based pay, taxable benefits, and Line 310 prior-year unpaid wages) in Box 852 multiplied by the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED in Box 854, where Box 854 is capped at a maximum of 75% (even if the specified employee actually spent 80% or 100% of their time directly engaged in SR&ED); and
Box 858 (The 2.5 × YMPE Cap): Calculated using the statutory formula:

body.text: Maximum Proxy Base Salary = 2.5 × YMPE × (Number of Days Employed in Tax Year ÷ 365)

Under Regulation 2900(7), this 2.5 × YMPE limit is prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for the time during the year that the employee was not a specified employee), and if the specified employee is also employed by an associated corporation, the maximum allowed cannot exceed 2.5 × YMPE minus the amount the associated corporation has included in its salary base for its taxation year ending in the same calendar year.

body.text: 4. The 180-Day Unpaid Remuneration Rule (Subsection 78(4))

Under subsection 78(4) of the Income Tax Act, if employee salary or wages accrued and incurred in a taxation year remain unpaid 180 days after the end of that taxation year, the expenditure is deemed not to have been incurred in that year; instead, it is deemed to be incurred in the subsequent taxation year in which the amount is actually paid. A payment made on the exact 180th day is accepted by the CRA as paid within the time limit, and two narrow statutory exceptions (reasonable vacation or holiday pay and deferred amounts under a salary deferral arrangement as defined in subsection 248(1)) are deemed paid on the 180th day.

Whether an amount was paid within 180 days is a question of fact evidenced by timely remittance of payroll source deductions (within 15 days after the month withheld), issuance of a T4 slip, employee income reporting, cancelled cheques, cash transfers, journal entries crediting the employee's account, directors' resolutions, or promissory notes (only if an agreement clearly establishes the note was accepted as absolute payment). Unpaid wages must be identified on Line 315 of Form T661 in the taxation year incurred and subsequently claimed on Line 310 in the taxation year paid. Crucially, under Regulation 2900(9), prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310) as well as the two 180th-day exceptions are excluded from the Proxy Salary Base, permanently forfeiting the 55% PPA on those amounts. Furthermore, as held in Jaft Corp. (2015 MBCA 77), wages that are contingently payable only if the SR&ED claim is approved by the CRA are disallowed.
5. Permissible Foreign SR&ED Salaries Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) — The 10% Limit)

Following the litigation in LGL Ltd. v. The Queen (2000 FCA), where the courts strictly enforced the territorial boundary of Canada (and its Exclusive Economic Zone [EEZ]) for data collection, Parliament enacted subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) to permit a limited claim for SR&ED work performed by employees physically outside Canada. To claim foreign SR&ED wages on Line 307 (non-specified employees) or Line 309 (specified employees), four cumulative statutory conditions must be satisfied:

items: The work must be performed directly by an employee of the claimant (foreign subcontractor payments are 100% ineligible) who was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred;
The SR&ED work must be related to a business of the claimant;
The foreign SR&ED work must be an integral part of, and solely in support of, an SR&ED project carried on by the claimant inside Canada; and
The salary or wages paid must not be subject to income or profits tax from another country.

body.text: The total permissible foreign SR&ED salary (Line 307 + Line 309) is capped at the lesser of the actual eligible foreign SR&ED wages (Amount A) and 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages for SR&ED performed in Canada (Amount B). Under the Proxy Method, Amount B equals 10% of Line 306 (directly engaged Canadian SR&ED salaries). Under the Traditional Method, Amount B equals 10% of the sum of Line 306 plus the salaries of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support the SR&ED claimed on Line 360.
3.2 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), Regulation 2900(2)(a), and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy (updated March 27, 2026), claimants under both the Traditional and Proxy methods may claim the cost of materials either consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

"Materials for SR&ED" refers to all raw materials, substances, or other physical, tangible items (solid, liquid, or gaseous) that compose the body of a tangible object at a given moment in the SR&ED process. The claimable cost includes the original laid-down invoice cost to acquire the item plus all reasonable costs to bring that item to its condition and location to be consumed or transformed in SR&ED in Canada (including in-house production overhead expenses for materials manufactured by the claimant, even when using the Proxy Method). Crucially, materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are physically consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, not when they are purchased from a supplier or removed from inventory.

Materials Consumed (Line 320) are materials that are destroyed, absorbed, used up, broken down, or rendered virtually valueless (scrap value ≤10% of cost) as a result of the SR&ED. Materials consumed are not subject to ITC recapture unless subsequent proceeds received (such as insurance proceeds) exceed 10% of the cost. Materials Transformed (Line 325) are input materials or component parts used in experimental testing or experimental production (ED+EP) that are changed or incorporated into another material or product and are not rendered virtually valueless. If materials transformed (including agricultural animals or growing things on which incremental SR&ED feed, fertilizer, or chemical costs were claimed, excluding control groups) are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, they trigger ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36).

Costs of general utilities (water, fuel, electricity, oil) are not considered materials for SR&ED and are claimable only as overhead under the Traditional Method, except for energy costs incurred in endothermic chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, metallurgical, or biotechnology reactions where the energy physically transforms or composes the materials. Finally, under subsection 127(11.6), when materials are purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes is restricted to the "adjusted selling cost" incurred by the related supplier, stripping out any intercompany profit markup (reported as an adjustment on Line 542).
3.3 Overhead Methodologies: The Proxy Method (55% PPA) vs. The Traditional Method

Under subsection 37(8) and subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must elect annually on its first Form T661 filed for the taxation year between the Proxy Method (Line 160) and the Traditional Method (Line 162). Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the election is binding and irrevocable for that year. If a claimant fails to make a selection on Form T661, the CRA processes the claim using the Traditional Method.
1. The Proxy Method and the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

Elected by the vast majority of Canadian SR&ED claimants, the Proxy Method eliminates the need to specifically identify, track, and allocate individual overhead expenses. Instead, under Regulation 2900(4) and the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy (updated April 28, 2022), the claimant computes a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 equal to 55% of the SR&ED Salary Base (Line 820, carried to Line 502):
Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) = 55% × Salary Base (Line 818)

The PPA rate was 65% for taxation years ending in 2012 and prior years, 60% for 2013, and has been fixed at 55% since 2014. Under Clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) and Regulations 2900(7)–(9), the Salary Base (Line 818) equals the directly engaged SR&ED salaries of non-specified employees (Line 810) minus all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (Line 812, yielding Subtotal Line 814), plus the allowable directly engaged salaries of specified employees from Box 860 (Line 816, subject to the 75% time cap and 2.5 × YMPE limit).

The PPA is added directly to Qualified SR&ED Expenditures on Line 502 to earn the federal (and applicable provincial) ITC under subsection 127(9), but it is never added to the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. Instead, the actual overhead expenses that the PPA represents (support staff wages, office supplies, utilities, travel, training, maintenance) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the Income Tax Act. Furthermore, Part 5 Section B enforces an Overall Cap on the PPA to ensure that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and other specific Income Tax Act deductions do not exceed total business expenditures made in the taxation year. The Overall Cap is calculated by taking total deductions for income tax purposes (total expenses per the income statement minus Schedule T2SCH1 expense additions plus Schedule T2SCH1 expense deductions) and subtracting deductions allowed under other sections of the Act—specifically Capital Cost Allowance (Schedule T2SCH8), the Section 37 SR&ED deduction claimed in the year (Schedule T2SCH1, Line 411), building rent, and interest.
2. The Traditional Method (Directly Related and Incremental Overheads)

Under clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and Regulations 2900(2) and 2900(3), a claimant electing the Traditional Method does not compute a PPA; instead, it specifically identifies, tracks, allocates, and claims actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. These amounts are added to both the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and the Section 127 Qualified Expenditure Pool for ITC purposes.

Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022) and Regulations 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3)(b), every overhead expenditure (or reasonably allocated portion thereof, such as square-footage allocation for facility municipal taxes or building insurance) claimed under the Traditional Method must satisfy two cumulative statutory tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must connect directly—with no intervening step or intermediary—to one of three elements: (a) the SR&ED work itself, (b) the SR&ED staff, or (c) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED.

The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED (or the provision of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment) not occurred. Fixed costs (such as a fixed-cost maintenance contract) fail the incremental test, whereas variable electricity or maintenance costs that increase directly with SR&ED equipment usage qualify.

body.text: Under the Traditional Method, potentially eligible incremental overhead costs include salaries of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support SR&ED (other than directly engaged), contract costs for non-SR&ED trades (such as electricians, welders, and mechanics) directly related and incremental to SR&ED, moving expenses to relocate selected candidates or SR&ED employees within Canada, taxable benefits related to hiring SR&ED personnel (such as housing loss coverage), travel and training in Canada, utilities, telephone/internet, periodical subscriptions, clinical study volunteer fees, health and safety expenses, ongoing SR&ED waste disposal, and variable equipment repair and maintenance. Conversely, Regulation 2902 and CRA policy strictly exclude general corporate administration, legal and accounting fees (including SR&ED claim preparation fees), patent application costs, bidding and licensing expenses, non-technological feasibility studies, headhunter fees, hiring advertisements, immigration/visa costs, conventions and conferences, interest, and Capital Cost Allowance.
