body.text: 3.4 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's Length Contracts, and Third-Party Payments
1. Arm's Length SR&ED Contracts (Line 340 — The 80% Rule)

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and the CRA's Contract Expenditures for SR&ED Performed on Behalf of a Claimant Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a claimant may engage an arm's length contractor to perform SR&ED (or eligible paragraph 248(1)(d) support work commensurate with the claimant's SR&ED) in Canada on behalf of the claimant. Work is performed "on behalf of" the payer when the payer controls the technical specifications and direction of the work, bears the financial and technical risk, and typically retains exclusive ownership of the resulting intellectual property.

While 100% of an eligible arm's length contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool, under subsection 127(9) only 80% of the expenditure qualifies for the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (since January 1, 2013, effected by entering a 20% reduction on Line 529 of Form T661). If a contract expenditure (or other non-wage current expenditure) remains unpaid 180 days after taxation year-end under subsection 127(26), the 80% unpaid portion is deducted on Line 520 in the year incurred and added back on Line 500 in the subsequent taxation year when paid.

To qualify for an ITC, the contractor must be a taxable supplier under subsection 127(9)—meaning a person resident in Canada or a non-resident carrying on business in Canada through a permanent establishment subject to Part I Canadian income tax. Payments to non-taxable suppliers (such as foreign subcontractors without a Canadian permanent establishment) are deducted on Line 528 and earn 0% ITC. If a single arm's length contract covers both SR&ED and commercial work (for example, a $300,000 custom development contract where $125,000 is allocated to SR&ED and $175,000 to commercial work), only the $125,000 SR&ED portion enters the Section 37 pool, and 80% of that amount ($100,000) earns an ITC. Finally, following the Bill C-15 restoration of capital expenditures after December 15, 2024, the former capital look-through rule in subsections 37(14) and 37(15) no longer reduces contract expenditures or third-party payments for performer capital costs incurred after December 15, 2024.
2. Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts (Line 345, Line 541, and Form T1146)

Under subsections 37(13), 127(9) (paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure"), 127(13), and 127(24), when a claimant (payer) contracts SR&ED work to a non-arm's length performer (such as a sister or subsidiary corporation under section 251), the contract payment is an allowable Section 37 deductible expenditure to the payer (entered on Line 345), but is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures (deducted in full on Line 541) and earns 0% ITC directly for the payer.

Because the transaction is between non-arm's length parties, subsection 127(9) excludes the receipt from the definition of a "contract payment", allowing the NAL performer to claim its own underlying SR&ED salaries, materials, and PPA without any contract payment reduction. Furthermore, under subsection 37(13), if a NAL performer is contracted to perform only paragraph 248(1)(d) support work linked to SR&ED performed by the related payer, that support work is eligible in the hands of the NAL performer. Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer (transferor) and NAL payer (transferee) can jointly execute and file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures (capped at the performer's year-end qualified expenditure pool) to the payer (reported on Line 508 / Line 510 by the transferee and Line 540 by the transferor). When purchasing non-contract goods or services from a NAL supplier, subsections 127(11.6) to 127(11.8) limit the buyer's qualified expenditure to the supplier's "adjusted selling cost" or "adjusted service cost" (Line 542).
3. Third-Party Payments (Line 370 and Form T1263)

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) and 37(1)(a)(ii) and the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy (updated March 30, 2022), a third-party payment is a payment made to an approved university, college, research institute, association, granting council, non-profit SR&ED corporation, or other resident corporation for SR&ED carried on in Canada where the work is controlled by the performer rather than undertaken on behalf of the claimant.

To qualify, the SR&ED must be carried on in Canada, must relate to a business of the claimant, and the claimant must be entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED (non-exclusive rights suffice, provided the claimant gains a preferential right to use the results in its business as a direct result of the payment). Unconditional payments in kind to a university or college are valued at fair market value, and agricultural producer levies paid through agricultural organizations are treated as direct third-party payments by the producers. Unlike SR&ED contracts (which are recognized on an accrual basis), third-party payments are deducted on a cash basis when paid (subject to subsection 18(9) prepaid expense limitations), are reduced by 20% on Line 529 (so that 80% earns an ITC), and require Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) to be attached for each payment.
3.5 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), Leased Equipment, and Software/Cloud Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

After being excluded from the SR&ED program between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital equipment purchases and equipment lease costs were fully restored by Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) for property acquired and available for use (or lease costs incurred) after December 15, 2024.
1. All or Substantially All (ASA ≥90%) Capital Property (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Line 390)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure (reported on Line 390 and listed on Lines 262–263 for the 10 most expensive properties per project) if, at the time it was incurred, the claimant intended that:

items: The property would be used during all or substantially all (ASA, ≥90%) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada; or
All or substantially all (≥90%) of its value would be consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada.

body.text: Under subsections 37(1.2) and 127(11.2), capital property is deemed not to have been acquired until it becomes available for use by the claimant. While the Bill C-15 coming-into-force rule for section 37 applies to property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, tax practitioners have noted that because subsection 127(11.2) deems capital expenditures not to be incurred for ITC purposes until the property is available for use, equipment ordered prior to December 16, 2024, that first became operational and available for use after December 15, 2024, raises a technical timing question under subsection 127(11.2).

Qualifying ASA capital expenditures are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool (deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance) and must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (CCA). For a qualifying CCPC or ECPC within the $6 million expenditure limit, ASA capital expenditures earn the 35% enhanced ITC, of which 40% is refundable in cash. Non-depreciable property (land, inventory, goodwill) and buildings (including leasehold interests in buildings) are strictly excluded under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e). Under Regulation 2902(b), General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) (desks, chairs, photocopiers, standard phones) is excluded under the Proxy Method, but allowable under the Traditional Method if used ≥90% for SR&ED. Crucially, computers, hardware, software, and ancillary electronic equipment are explicitly not considered GPOEF and qualify under both methods. Used equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, can be deducted in the Section 37 pool (Line 390), but is prescribed under Regulation 2902 as ineligible for the Section 127 ITC unless refurbished so significantly after December 15, 2024, that it is considered new when acquired.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE — Subsection 127(9), Line 504, and Part 6C)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026), if a claimant acquires new depreciable equipment after December 15, 2024, that fails the ≥90% ASA test because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial operations, it can still earn a partial SR&ED ITC as Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) (reported on Line 504 and listed in Part 6C, Box 788 for the 20 most expensive SUE items) if it is used primarily (more than 50% and less than 90%) of its actual operating time for SR&ED in Canada (and is not GPOEF or a Prescribed Depreciable Property).

SUE operates across two statutory evaluation windows. The First Period (First-Term SUE) begins when the equipment is acquired (available for use) and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after acquisition; if actual operating logs show >50% SR&ED usage over that First Period, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (determined without borrowed money costs under section 21 and adjusted for NAL suppliers under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 504 in that taxation year. The Second Period (Second-Term SUE) begins on the original acquisition date and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition; if cumulative actual operating logs over the entire Second Period exceed 50% SR&ED usage, an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (for a cumulative 50% of capital cost) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC on Line 504.

For example, as illustrated in Section 3.5 of the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy, if a calendar-year corporation purchases a new $300,000 machine available for use on January 2, 2025, the period to December 31, 2025, is less than 12 months, so no SUE ITC is claimed in 2025 (the asset is added to its regular CCA class on Schedule T2SCH8). By December 31, 2026 (the end of the First Period, at least 12 months after January 2, 2025), if the machine logged 2,900 SR&ED hours out of 3,600 total operating hours (81% SR&ED use), the company claims First-Term SUE of 25% × $300,000 = $75,000 on Line 504 in 2026. By December 31, 2027 (the end of the Second Period, at least 24 months after January 2, 2025), if cumulative usage is 3,700 SR&ED hours out of 5,600 total hours (66% SR&ED use), the company claims Second-Term SUE of another 25% × $300,000 = $75,000 on Line 504 in 2027.

Unlike ASA capital property, SUE capital cost never enters the Section 37 pool; instead, the claimant depreciates 100% of the asset under normal CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8, and any SUE ITC applied or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the following taxation year. Under Regulation 2900(11), property is disqualified as Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) if, at acquisition, the claimant intended to use it for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing facility, plant, or line and intended its primary use over its expected useful life to be non-SR&ED (though pilot plant equipment and unexpected troubleshooting on a replacement commercial machine are not PDP).
3. Equipment Lease Expenditures and Software/Cloud Licences (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026), lease payments incurred after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada qualify according to the method elected (measured across the full 12-month taxation year, or the post-December 15, 2024 operating time for straddle taxation years). Under the Proxy Method (subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI)), excluding GPOEF and land leases, if leased equipment is used ASA (≥90%) of its operating time in SR&ED, 100% of the lease cost is claimable; if used primarily (>50% to <90%), 50% of the lease cost is claimable; and if used ≤50%, 0% is claimable. Under the Traditional Method (subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II) and Regulation 2900(2)(c)), if leased equipment (including GPOEF and land leases) is used ASA (≥90%) in SR&ED, 100% is claimable as a lease cost; if used <90%, the proportional percentage of SR&ED usage is claimable as an overhead expenditure on Line 360, provided the lease is directly related and incremental to SR&ED.

Outlays for the use or right to use a building (rent) are strictly disallowed under paragraph 37(8)(e), except for a prescribed special-purpose building as defined in Regulation 2903 (though non-building structures such as bridges or dams may qualify). Conversely, because computers and software are not GPOEF, expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024, for scientific, engineering, or development software and software licences (as well as dedicated bandwidth leases under Section 4.3.1 of the Lease Policy) qualify as either SR&ED capital expenditures or current lease/right-to-use expenditures depending on the terms of the licence.
4. Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and ITC Recapture Mechanics
4.1 Government and Non-Government Assistance & Contract Payments (Subsections 127(9), 127(18)–(20), and Paragraph 37(1)(d))

To ensure that a claimant earns SR&ED tax incentives only on its net out-of-pocket R&D expenditure, paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) and 127(19) of the Income Tax Act (administered under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy) require both the Section 37 Pool and the Section 127 Qualified Expenditure Pool to be reduced by all government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of its income tax return for the taxation year.
1. Government and Non-Government Assistance

Under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x), government assistance means assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including a Crown corporation, foreign government, or government-funded non-profit organization) whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself. Non-government assistance means any inducement, reimbursement, contribution, or allowance received from a private entity that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (read without reference to subparagraphs 12(1)(x)(v) to (vii)).
Three major categories of government assistance routinely reduce federal SR&ED claims:

items: Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credits: Provincial R&D credits (such as the Ontario OITC/ORDTC/OBRITC, Québec CRIC, BC SR&ED credit, Alberta IEG, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon credits) constitute government assistance and reduce the federal Section 37 pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures.

Direct R&D Grants and Wage Subsidies: Non-repayable contributions from the National Research Council Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) (which covers up to 80% of R&D salaries up to $500,000 per project), Student Work Placement Program (SWPP) subsidies, or emergency wage subsidies (such as CEWS) reduce the specific SR&ED project expenditures they fund.

Forgivable and Conditional / "Patient" Government Loans (Immunovaccine and CAE Inc. Precedents): If a government loan lacks firm, unconditional commercial repayment terms—for example, if repayment is contingent on future project revenues or profits, or features a multi-year deferral of interest and principal without a commercial "for-profit" target rate of return (such as loans under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative [SADI])—the CRA and the courts classify the full loan advance as government assistance (a forgivable loan) that grinds down SR&ED qualified expenditures in the year received, as affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. The Queen (2014 FCA 196; aff'g 2013 TCC 103) and CAE Inc. v. The Queen (2022 FCA; aff'g 2021 TCC). When the loan or assistance is subsequently repaid in future years, the repayment is added back to the Section 37 pool (Line 445) and generates an ITC in the year repaid at the historical rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the claim. By contrast, under subsection 12(11) and the clean economy investment tax credit provisions—sections 127.44 (Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage ITC), 127.45 (Clean Technology ITC), 127.48 (Clean Hydrogen ITC), 127.49 (Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC), and 127.491 (Clean Electricity ITC)—statutory "excluded loan" definitions and anti-stacking rules govern the interaction between clean economy incentives and government assistance.

body.text: Assistance reduces expenditures on a project-by-project basis down to nil; however, under subsection 127(19), if assistance and contract payments exceed a project's qualified expenditures, the excess reduces the qualified expenditures of any non-arm's length party performing work on the same project. Under subsection 127(20), non-arm's length group members may file Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) on or before the transferor's filing-due date (or within the Notice of Objection period) to allocate assistance among group members.
2. Contract Payments vs. Commercial Revenue (Com Dev Ltd. Precedent)

Under subsection 127(9), a contract payment is an amount paid or payable to a claimant by an arm's length taxable supplier (or by a Canadian government, municipality, public authority, or tax-exempt entity) for SR&ED to be performed for it or on its behalf. A contract payment reduces the performer's qualified expenditures so that both the customer and the performer cannot claim ITCs on the same work.

However, as established in the landmark Tax Court decision Com Dev Ltd. v. The Queen (96-4343-IT-G, 1999 TCC) and Section 5.5 of the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, a fixed-price contract to deliver a commercial product or custom good is ordinary commercial revenue—not a contract payment—allowing the performer to retain 100% of its SR&ED ITCs. The CRA evaluates four criteria in Section 5.5 to distinguish a contract payment from commercial revenue: (1) Contractor performance requirements (whether the contract explicitly requires performing SR&ED on the customer's behalf or delivering a functional good); (2) Pricing vs. risks assumed (whether the performer bears the financial risk of cost overruns under a fixed-price structure, as in Com Dev, or is reimbursed on a cost-plus basis); (3) Intellectual property ownership (whether the performer retains IP rights or assigns exclusive IP to the payer); and (4) Contract for services vs. contract for the sale of goods.
4.2 Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36))

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (updated October 14, 2022), if a taxpayer claims an SR&ED ITC on the cost of a property (such as materials transformed, post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use Equipment, pre-2014 capital equipment, or property acquired via an arm's length SR&ED contract) and subsequently sells that property or converts it to commercial use within 20 taxation years of acquisition, the ITC must be recaptured and added directly to the taxpayer's Part I income tax payable.
The Four Statutory Triggers (Subsection 127(27))
Recapture is triggered in a taxation year when all four statutory conditions are present:

items: The claimant acquired a particular property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 to 20 years by subsection 127(36));
The cost of the property was a qualified expenditure of the claimant;
All or a percentage of the cost of the property was included in computing the claimant's SR&ED ITC at the end of a taxation year; and
In the taxation year, the claimant converts the property (or another property that incorporates the property) to commercial use, or disposes of it.

The Recovery Value Multiplied by the Historical ITC Rate:

where the Historical ITC Rate is the exact percentage rate (such as 35%, 15%, or the pre-2014 20% rate) applied when calculating the original ITC earned on the property.
Critical Audit Nuances of ITC Recapture

Under subsection 127(32), the "cost" of a property for recapture purposes cannot exceed the amount paid by the claimant to acquire the property. Consequently, as illustrated in Section 7.1.1 of the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a claimant manufactures a prototype or component in-house, recapture applies only to the cost of the purchased materials transformed; there is no recapture on the internal SR&ED salaries or overhead costs incurred to manufacture the part. Conversely, if the claimant orders that same part from an arm's length supplier for $12,000 (comprising $10,000 of supplier manufacturing/development costs plus a $2,000 profit margin), the entire $12,000 purchase price represents the property cost subject to recapture.

By administrative policy (Section 6.2 of the Recapture Policy), the CRA applies a 10% de minimis rule: recapture will not be applied when the proceeds from a scrap sale or the fair market value of an SR&ED output upon commercial conversion is less than 10% of the total cost of the property (or ≤10% for materials consumed). Any amount added to Part I tax payable under the recapture rules can be offset by unused current or carryforward SR&ED ITCs, and increases the claimant's Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures for the following taxation year (Line 453). Finally, under subsections 127(28) to 127(35), special recapture rules govern partnerships (where recapture first reduces partnership ITCs before flowing through to partners), transferred NAL expenditures under subsection 127(29) (where the performer recaptures the ITC if the property is sold or converted to commercial use), and NAL transfers of ASA capital property under subsections 127(33) and 127(34) (where recapture is deferred on a NAL transfer if the transferee continues to use the property all or substantially all for SR&ED).
5. Special Taxpayer Structures: Partnerships, Joint Ventures, and Trusts
5.1 Partnerships (Section 96 and Subsection 127(8))

Because a partnership is not a distinct legal "person" or "taxpayer" under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, special flow-through rules govern SR&ED performed by partnerships, as codified in the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy (updated April 28, 2022):

items: Mandatory Current-Year Pool Deduction (Paragraph 96(1)(e.1)): Under subsection 96(1), net income is computed at the partnership level as if the partnership were a separate person, but paragraph 96(1)(e.1) mandates that 100% of the partnership's Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures must be deducted in full in the fiscal period incurred. A partnership cannot carry forward an undeducted Section 37 pool balance to a future year.

Ineligibility of Partner Remuneration: For income tax purposes, a partner cannot be an employee of the partnership. Any salary or wages paid to a partner is treated by the CRA as a distribution of partnership income—not a deductible employment expense—and cannot be claimed as an SR&ED expenditure.

Loss of Enhanced 35% CCPC Rate (All Colour Chemicals Rule): Under subsection 127(8), SR&ED ITCs are calculated at the partnership level and then allocated to eligible partners on T5013 slips. Because a partnership is not a CCPC, the subsection 127(10.1) 20% enhancement does not apply to partnership expenditures; thus, even if all partners are CCPCs, the partnership only earns the 15% basic ITC rate (as held in All Colour Chemicals).

Exclusion of Limited Partners and "Specified Members": Under subsections 96(2.1) and 127(8), a limited partner or a specified member (a partner who is not regularly, continuously, and substantially actively engaged in the partnership's business activities during the fiscal period, other than financing, or carrying on a similar business) cannot be allocated any SR&ED ITCs, and any partnership loss attributable to the Section 37 SR&ED deduction is denied to the limited partner (and does not become a limited partnership loss, non-capital loss, or adjusted cost base reduction).

No Non-Arm's Length Transfers (Form T1146): Because subsection 127(13) applies only to "persons" and a partnership is not a person for this purpose, a partnership cannot transfer or receive qualified SR&ED expenditures using Form T1146.

body.text: 5.2 Joint Ventures vs. Partnerships

Unlike a partnership, a joint venture does not compute net income at the joint venture level and does not file a T5013 partnership information return. As stated in the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, each joint venture participant files its own separate SR&ED claim on its own Form T661 for the SR&ED work it performed, contracted on its behalf, or funded via third-party payments, thereby allowing a CCPC participant in a joint venture to retain full access to the 35% enhanced refundable ITC rate and Section 37 pool carryforwards.

body.text: Strict Judicial Enforcement of the 18-Month Deadline

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12), the 18-month corporate filing deadline is an absolute statutory bar: since legislative amendments enacted on November 17, 2005 (which removed ministerial discretion to extend SR&ED deadlines), neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada has authority to extend the 18-month deadline. If a corporation's tax year ends on the last day of a month (for example, December 31, 2025, or February 28), its T2 return is due on the last day of the 6th month (June 30, 2026, or August 31), and its SR&ED reporting deadline is the last day of the 18th month (June 30, 2027, or August 31 of the following year); if the tax year ends on a day other than the last day of a month (for example, January 6), the deadline is the exact same day of the 18th month (July 6 of the following year).

If a claimant files Form T661 within 18 months but fails to file Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) by the 18-month deadline, the expenditures can enter the Section 37 deduction pool, but the ITC is permanently lost, as affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Easy Way Cattle Oilers Ltd. v. The Queen (2016 FCA; aff'g 2015 TCC 211). Furthermore, a letter expressing an "intent to file", an unsubstantiated estimate, or a filing by a related company on the wrong corporate return (as in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 9; aff'd 2018 FCA) does not satisfy subsection 37(11). If the CRA contacts a claimant regarding missing prescribed information on a filed Form T661, the claimant must submit the missing information before the 18-month deadline expires; once the 18th month passes, the CRA cannot accept missing prescribed line items.
Architecture of the 2026 Form T661 and the $1,000 Claim Preparer Penalty (Subsection 162(5.1))
The updated Form T661 (released May 15, 2026, alongside updated Forms T1145 and T1146 on May 15, 2026, Schedule T2SCH31 on May 22, 2026, and Schedule T2SCH49 on May 29, 2026) comprises 10 parts:

items: Part 1 — General Information: Business Name (Line 010), 15-character Business Number, total number of projects (Line 050), financial contact (Lines 100–110), and technical contact (Lines 115–125).

Section B captures the three core technical narrative responses (subject to strict word limits and written by or in the technical language of the personnel who did the work): Line 242 (scientific or technological uncertainties attempted to be overcome), Line 244 (work performed in the tax year, including hypotheses, experiments/analyses, results, and conclusions), and Line 246 (scientific or technological advancements achieved or attempted). Under subsection 162(5.1), if required Part 9 claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or false, a $1,000 penalty is assessed per claim, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable. Crucially, as clarified in the CRA's January 28, 2025 SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, Part 9 is not subject to the subsection 37(11) forfeiture deadline: an SR&ED claim will not be disallowed if Part 9 is the only missing or inaccurate information, though the $1,000 penalty under subsection 162(5.1) applies.
6.2 The 2026 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322)

Launched on April 1, 2026, under the Bill C-15 administrative reforms, the CRA's Pre-Claim Approval Process allows eligible businesses (corporations or partnerships with gross business income below $25 million) to obtain a formal, upfront technical determination from the CRA confirming whether their planned R&D projects qualify as SR&ED before starting work or incurring costs.

To apply, the business first requests a Pre-Claim Approval Case Number (entered on Line 016) via My Business Account and then completes and submits Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Pre-Claim Approval) for up to 3 planned projects (Line 014) covering a pre-claim approval period of up to 3 years. In Part 2 Section A of Form T1322, the applicant provides the project title (Line 020), anticipated project start date (Line 022), estimated total SR&ED expenditures (Line 024), field of science or technology code (Line 026), and technical contact person (Lines 028–032). In Part 2 Section B of Form T1322, the applicant must answer three detailed technical questions within strict word limits:

items: Line 042 (Maximum 500 words): What scientific or technological uncertainty do you aim to address (stating the business context, project objective, and new knowledge or capability sought)?

Line 043 (Maximum 700 words): What due diligence have you completed to confirm that the scientific or technological uncertainty described in Line 042 cannot be resolved using existing knowledge, solutions, or approaches (detailing literature reviews, patents, vendor documentation, expert consultations, and preliminary trials)?

Line 044 (Maximum 900 words): What work do you plan to perform during the pre-claim approval period (up to 3 years) to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainty described at Line 042 (detailing hypotheses, planned experiments/analyses, and any external contractors or specialized testing services)?

body.text: In Section D of Form T1322, the applicant must upload four categories of supporting business documentation through My Business Account: (1) project planning documents (timelines, milestones, Gantt charts, work breakdown structures); (2) a description of planned internal controls for time-tracking and contemporaneous experimental record-keeping; (3) key supporting due-diligence references and design documents; and (4) a list of project team members with their credentials and expertise. Following a technical meeting with the applicant's technical contact, the CRA provides a formal determination within 8 weeks. When the claimant subsequently files its annual Form T661, if the claim is selected for review and includes only pre-approved projects that have not materially changed, the CRA restricts its review to verifying expenditures and processes the refundable claim within 90 calendar days.
6.3 CRA Review Timelines, Audit Procedures, Penalties, and Dispute Resolution
1. CRA Refund Processing Service Standards
Once a complete claim and income tax return are received, the CRA applies three service standards to refundable claims (no service standard applies to non-refundable claims):

items: Within 60 Calendar Days: Refundable claims Accepted as Filed (AAF) without review.
Within 90 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for review that include only projects granted Pre-Claim Approval (where the work remains as approved).
Within 180 Calendar Days: Refundable claims selected for review that include any project not granted Pre-Claim Approval or that materially differs from what was previously granted pre-claim approval.

body.text: 2. First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS) and Coordinated Technical/Financial Reviews

If a business is submitting its first SR&ED claim or has not submitted a claim in the preceding 3 years, it may be selected for the First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS)—a mandatory CRA service that provides personalized recommendations and guidance to improve future claim compliance. When a past FTCAS recipient is later reviewed, the RTA verifies whether the FTCAS report recommendations were addressed.

When a claim is selected for a technical and financial review, the CRA assigns a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (governed by the Claim Review Manual [CRM] for RTAs) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (governed by the Financial Claim Review Manual [FCRM]). Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated April 20, 2026) and the CRM, the review proceeds in three structured steps: (Step 1) Initial phone contact to introduce the RTA and FR, outline identified issues and selected projects, request supporting documents, and schedule the review meeting; (Step 2) The review meeting (virtual or on-site), featuring interviews with technical and financial staff, a virtual or physical tour of the premises, examination of dated contemporaneous technical evidence and financial ledgers, and sharing of preliminary findings; and (Step 3) Issuance of the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report and Proposal Package (if adjustments or penalties are proposed), giving the claimant 30 days to submit written representations and additional evidence before a final assessment or reassessment is issued. Under the CRM, RTAs must adhere to eight due-process principles under the Taxpayer Bill of Rights, record all working papers in the TF98 file, consult their Research and Technology Manager (RTM) before making an unfavourable decision without an on-site visit or disallowing a claim for lack of information, and must never negotiate eligibility or expenditures.
3. Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims (Subsection 163(2))

Under subsection 163(2) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05), if a claimant knowingly, or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence, makes a false statement or omission in an SR&ED claim, the CRA may assess a monetary gross negligence penalty. As noted in The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants, the mere presence of an error or disallowance is not sufficient to apply a gross negligence penalty; the CRA bears the burden of establishing that the false statement or omission was made knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence (and in criminal fraud prosecutions, courts have imposed fines of 150% to 300% of the claimed amount, as in R. v. Elhami, 2017 QCCQ 2684 and Tempora).
4. Three-Step Administrative Dispute Resolution, Notice of Objection, and Tax Court Appeal

Under the CRA's Guidelines for Resolving Claimants' SR&ED Concerns, disputes during a review follow a three-step internal escalation process: (Step 1) Speak directly with the RTA and/or FR; (Step 2) Escalate unresolved issues to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM); and (Step 3) Request an Administrative Review after receiving the Proposal Package. Following the issuance of a Notice of Assessment or Notice of Reassessment, the claimant has 90 calendar days to file a formal Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch, and may subsequently appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (and thereafter to the Federal Court of Appeal).
7. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and IP Box Incentives (2026 Landscape)

Nine Canadian provinces and one territory (Yukon) offer dedicated R&D tax credits that stack on top of the federal SR&ED program, while three jurisdictions—Prince Edward Island (PEI), the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut—offer no provincial or territorial R&D tax credit. Except for Québec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration [TRA]), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) via supplemental T2 schedules.
7.1 Québec: The Landmark 2025–2026 CRIC Overhaul, CDAEIA, and IDCI IP Box
1. Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC — Form RD-1029.8.CR-T)

Announced in the Québec 2025–2026 Budget (Information Bulletin 2025-6) and enacted for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec overhauled its R&D tax incentive landscape by introducing the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation — CRIC). For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the CRIC abolished and replaced the legacy Québec R&D tax measures: (1) the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers (which previously paid 30% enhanced / 14% basic for taxation years beginning on or before March 25, 2025); (2) the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium; (3) the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium; (4) the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research; (5) the tax credit for technological adaptation services; (6) the industrial design component of the design tax credits (while retaining the fashion design component); and (7) the tax holiday for foreign researchers and foreign experts.

Claimed on Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T, the CRIC is a 100% refundable tax credit available to any eligible corporation operating a business and maintaining an establishment in Québec, at a two-tier rate structure:

items: 30% Refundable Rate: On the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures that exceed the applicable exclusion threshold; and
20% Refundable Rate: On all qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 maximum.

body.text: While the CRIC's R&D definition is harmonized with federal SR&ED legislation (and scientifically reviewed by the CRA), the CRIC uniquely expands eligibility to cover pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization activities include: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation; (2) product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials; and (3) quality control activities related to implementing a quality control system required to obtain initial approval or certification.

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC comprise 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees, 100% of property acquisition costs (capital equipment / CAPEX) used in Québec (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings; cannot be combined with the Québec C3i credit or a large investment project tax holiday on the same property), 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec, and 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, research consortium, or university entity. Before calculating the credit, qualified expenditures must exceed an annual applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec personal income tax Basic Personal Amount (for example, $18,571) for each eligible employee, adjusted for the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.
2. Replacement of CDAE with CDAEIA (2026 AI Integration Mandate)

For Québec IT corporations, the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE — 30% credit on eligible IT salaries, split 23% refundable / 7% non-refundable for fiscal years starting in 2025) was replaced for fiscal years starting after December 31, 2025, by the CDAEIA (Crédit d'impôt pour le développement des affaires électroniques intégrant l'intelligence artificielle). Requiring an annual Investissement Québec certificate and claimed with Revenu Québec, the CDAEIA targets corporations that integrate artificial intelligence features in a significant way, providing a 30% credit on eligible salaries above an exclusion threshold (split 22% refundable / 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% / 9% in 2027, and 20% / 10% from 2028).
3. Québec's IP Box: Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI)

Under Title VII.2.8, section 737.18.43 of the Quebec Taxation Act (CQLR c. I-3), Québec operates an IP box known as the Incentive Deduction for the Commercialization of Innovations (IDCI). The IDCI applies to qualified IP assets—specifically protected inventions (patents or certificates of supplementary protection applied for after March 17, 2016), protected plant varieties (applied for after March 10, 2020), and protected software—resulting from R&D carried out in whole or in part in Québec. The deduction equals qualified commercialization profits multiplied by the Québec nexus ratio; for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the nexus ratio is computed based on R&D expenditures giving entitlement to the CRIC (excluding pre-commercialization activities and without reduction for the CRIC exclusion threshold).
7.2 Ontario: OITC (8%), ORDTC (3.5%), and OBRITC (20%)
Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario conducting qualifying SR&ED in the province can claim up to three credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), all administered by the CRA:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96, Schedule T2SCH566): Provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (10% for tax years ending before June 1, 2016) on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures up to an annual $3,000,000 expenditure limit (worth up to $240,000 annually). Unlike the federal expenditure limit, Ontario's $3 million OITC expenditure limit phases out when prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, and also phases out when prior-year taxable paid-up capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38–45, Schedule T2SCH508): Provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (4.5% prior to June 1, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reduced by the amount of any OITC and OBRITC claimed). Unused ORDTC can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, and recapture applies. Because both the OITC and ORDTC reduce federal qualified expenditures as government assistance, a corporation may waive all or part of the ORDTC (or OITC) by delivering a written waiver with its T2 return within 6 months of year-end (or on an amended return).

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97, Schedule T2SCH568): Provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with a designated Eligible Research Institute (ERI).

body.text: 7.3 Western Provinces: British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, and Manitoba
1. British Columbia (Sections 97–103 of the Income Tax Act (BC), Form T666)

Administered by the CRA, British Columbia provides a 10% SR&ED tax credit on qualified BC expenditures. For CCPCs, the 10% credit is 100% refundable up to the expenditure limit; for expenditures above the limit and for non-CCPCs, the 10% credit is non-refundable and can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 10 years. In its February 17, 2026 budget, British Columbia confirmed full alignment with the federal Bill C-15 changes: covering restored capital equipment expenditures, raising the BC expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million, and raising the taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10M–$50M to $15 million–$75 million. Form T666 must be filed within 18 months of taxation year-end, and recapture applies.
2. Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG — Sections 26.95–26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act, AT1 Schedule 29 & Form AT4970)

Administered by Alberta TRA for expenditures incurred after December 31, 2020, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides qualified corporations with a 100% refundable payment on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta SR&ED spending (phased out between $10M and $50M of taxable capital): an 8% payment on eligible spending up to the corporation's base level of spending (calculated as average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding 2 years), and an enhanced 20% payment on incremental spending exceeding that base level. Claimed on AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970, the filing deadline is 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date (21 months after year-end), and recapture applies.
3. Saskatchewan: R&D Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH403) and SCII Patent Box

Under Sections 63–63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan) (claimed on Schedule T2SCH403 and administered by the CRA), Saskatchewan provides a 10% R&D tax credit: for CCPCs, 10% refundable on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures and 10% non-refundable above $1,000,000; for other corporations, 10% non-refundable on all eligible expenditures (with total annual credits capped at $1,000,000, and non-refundable credits carried back 3 years and forward 10 years). Alongside the R&D credit, the Saskatchewan Commercial Innovation Incentive (SCII — "Patent Box") reduces the provincial corporate income tax rate to 6% for 10 consecutive years on income from commercializing qualifying IP (patents, plant breeders' rights, trade secrets, and copyrighted computer programs/algorithms).
4. Manitoba (Section 7.3 of The Income Tax Act (Manitoba), Schedule T2SCH380)

Administered by the CRA on Schedule T2SCH380 (due 12 months after the T2 filing-due date), Manitoba provides a 15% R&D tax credit (reduced from 20% after April 11, 2017): for in-house R&D, one-half (7.5%) is refundable and one-half (7.5%) is non-refundable (carried back 3 years and forward 20 years); for R&D conducted under contract with a qualifying institute, 100% (15%) is refundable.
7.4 Atlantic Provinces and Yukon Territory (15% Fully Refundable Regimes)
Four jurisdictions provide flat 15% fully refundable R&D tax credits administered by the CRA with no expenditure caps and no CCPC restrictions:

items: Nova Scotia (Section 41 of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia), Schedule T2SCH340): 15% fully refundable credit for corporations; 18-month filing deadline after year-end; recapture applies; may be renounced within 6 months of year-end.
New Brunswick (Section 59 of the New Brunswick Income Tax Act, Schedule T2SCH360): 15% fully refundable credit for corporations; recapture applies.

Newfoundland and Labrador (Section 42 of the Income Tax Act, 2000 (NL), Schedule T2SCH301 [Corporations] / Form T1129 [Individuals]): 15% fully refundable credit for corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships; filing deadline is 12 months after the return filing-due date; uniquely, eligible expenditures are NOT reduced by other government or non-government assistance (except GST/HST input tax credits).

Yukon Territory (Section 15 of the Income Tax Act (Yukon), Schedule T2SCH442 [Corporations] / Form T1232 [Individuals]): 15% fully refundable credit on eligible R&D in Yukon, plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on amounts paid or payable to Yukon University.

body.text: 7.5 Worked Mathematical Models: Federal–Provincial Stacking and Assistance Grinding

Because provincial R&D tax credits are classified as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, they reduce the federal qualified expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar before the 35% (or 15%) federal ITC rate is applied. Consequently, a 35% federal rate plus a 15% provincial rate does not equal 50%; instead, the combined effective recovery rate is governed by the multiplicative grinding formula:
Combined Effective Rate = r<sub>prov</sub> + r<sub>fed</sub> × (1 − r<sub>prov</sub>)
Worked Example 1: SaaS CCPC in Ontario Using the Proxy Method ($400,000 Total Developer Payroll)

Consider an Ontario CCPC with prior-year taxable income below $500,000 and taxable capital below $15 million that pays its non-specified software developers $400,000 in base T4 salary during its 2026 taxation year, with contemporaneous time records showing that 75% of their hours were spent directly engaged in eligible SR&ED in Ontario. The allowable directly engaged SR&ED salaries on Line 300/306 equal $300,000 ($400,000 × 75%), and the Prescribed Proxy Amount at 55% on Line 820/502 adds $165,000 ($300,000 × 55%), producing unadjusted qualified SR&ED expenditures of $465,000.

First, the corporation computes its 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) on Schedule T2SCH566, which equals $37,200 (8% × $465,000). Under Scenario A (ORDTC Waived to Maximize Immediate Cash Refund), if the startup has no Ontario corporate income tax payable and waives the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC, total Ontario government assistance is $37,200. Subtracting $37,200 reduces net federal qualified expenditures on Line 570 to $427,800 ($465,000 − $37,200), generating a 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC of $149,730 (35% × $427,800). The total combined cash refund is $186,930 ($37,200 OITC + $149,730 federal ITC), representing 40.20% of the $465,000 qualified expenditure pool, or 62.31% of the $300,000 actual cash SR&ED payroll outlay.

Under Scenario B (ORDTC Claimed by a Profitable CCPC), the eligible expenditure base for the 3.5% ORDTC is first reduced by the $37,200 OITC to $427,800, yielding a non-refundable ORDTC of $14,973 (3.5% × $427,800) on Schedule T2SCH508. Total Ontario assistance (OITC + ORDTC) is $52,173 ($37,200 + $14,973), reducing net federal qualified expenditures to $412,827 ($465,000 − $52,173) and generating a 35% federal SR&ED ITC of $144,489.45. The total combined tax credits equal $196,662.45 ($37,200 OITC + $14,973 ORDTC + $144,489.45 federal ITC), representing 42.29% of qualified expenditures, or 65.55% of the $300,000 direct SR&ED salary outlay.
Worked Example 2: Nova Scotia / Atlantic CCPC vs. Foreign-Controlled Subsidiary ($1,000,000 Qualified Expenditures)

Consider $1,000,000 of qualified SR&ED current expenditures (including PPA) incurred in Nova Scotia (or New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, or Yukon at the 15% base rate). For a qualifying CCPC or ECPC (35% federal rate), the 15% provincial refundable credit yields $150,000 (15% × $1,000,000), which reduces the federal qualified expenditure base to $850,000 ($1,000,000 − $150,000). Applying the 35% federal refundable rate to $850,000 yields $297,500, resulting in a total combined cash refund of $447,500 ($150,000 + $297,500), or 44.75% of qualified expenditures (69.36% of direct SR&ED salaries when the 55% PPA applies). For a foreign-controlled subsidiary (15% federal basic rate), the 15% provincial credit still pays $150,000 in cash, while the 15% non-refundable federal ITC on the remaining $850,000 base yields $127,500 in federal tax offsets, for a total combined recovery of $277,500 (27.75% of qualified expenditures).
8. Landmark Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents (1988–2026)

Canadian SR&ED eligibility and compliance are governed by a mature body of common-law precedents from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA). Every CRA technical review report and Notice of Objection is evaluated against these judicial rulings.
8.1 Foundational Doctrines: The Five-Question Northwest Hydraulic Test

In Sass Manufacturing Ltd. v. M.N.R. (88 DTC 1363, 1988 TCC), the earliest modern Tax Court interpretation of the regulatory predecessor to subsection 248(1), the Court held that systematic investigation requires a structured, documented methodology of hypothesis formulation and testing rather than unrecorded shop-floor trial-and-error adjustments. Subsequently, in Consoltex Inc. v. The Queen (97 DTC 724, 1997 TCC), Associate Chief Justice Bowman established two foundational principles: first, because SR&ED provisions are enacted to encourage scientific research in Canada, they must be given "such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects" under section 12 of the Interpretation Act; and second, intuitive creativity and genius play a vital role within the discipline of the scientific method. Consoltex also allowed textile materials transformed during experimental production runs and later sold commercially, which directly prompted Parliament to enact the subsection 127(27) ITC recapture rules in 1998.

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. Her Majesty the Queen ([1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 TCC)—the single most important SR&ED judgment in Canadian legal history—Justice Bowman evaluated five hydraulic engineering physical modelling projects (allowing four of the five) and formulated the five-criteria test at paragraph 16 that remains the operative legal test for SR&ED eligibility across Canada:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? Justice Bowman defined "routine engineering" as "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field." If the resolution of a problem is reasonably predictable using standard procedures or routine engineering, no technological uncertainty exists.

Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? This entails a five-stage process: (a) observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulation of a clear objective; (c) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses.

Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses? Characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, recognizing that what may appear routine and obvious in hindsight may not have been before the work was undertaken.

Did the process result in a technological advancement? Defined as an advancement in general understanding available to persons knowledgeable in the field; crucially, the rejection of a hypothesis after testing is nonetheless an advancement because it eliminates a hitherto untested hypothesis.
Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (99 DTC 5087, [1998] F.C.J. No. 1890, 1998 FCA) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740), the Federal Court of Appeal elevated Justice Bowman's five Northwest Hydraulic criteria into binding appellate law. In RIS-Christie, the FCA held that while repeatability of tests is an essential hallmark of scientific research, documentary evidence—though practically indispensable—is not an absolute statutory prerequisite where credible oral or circumstantial evidence proves systematic testing (particularly in extreme circumstances where the key engineer died prior to trial).
8.2 Routine Engineering vs. Technological Uncertainty: Jentel, Joel Theatrical, and Kam-Press

In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261; aff'd 2011 FCA 355), a Calgary thermoforming manufacturer claimed SR&ED for overhauling its "Multi-Bins" small-parts storage system by testing eight known plastic resins (ABS, HDPE, PETG, PVC, Lexan, acrylic, styrene, polyethylene), wood and aluminum stands, snap-fit sliders, and plug-assist heat sinks. Justice D'Arcy dismissed the appeal (affirmed unanimously by the FCA), holding that testing existing, well-known materials and standard thermoforming techniques (such as plug-assist moulds that had been in industry use for years) to optimize product weight, strength, and cost constituted routine engineering and standard product development, not SR&ED. Furthermore, the Tax Court placed zero weight on opinion testimony offered by a witness who was not properly qualified as an independent expert.

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), Justice Sommerfeldt synthesized the jurisprudence on routine engineering and the scientific method, defining a "hypothesis" at paragraph 26 as "a statement to be tested by an experiment or a trial" and confirming at paragraph 33 that the scientific method requires (1) trained and systematic observation, (2) measurement and experiment, and (3) formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 246; aff'd 2021 FCA 88), the appellant argued before the Federal Court of Appeal that because the explicit words "scientific method" do not appear in the text of subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, the Tax Court erred in applying the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion. Writing for a unanimous FCA panel, Justice Webb dismissed the appeal with costs, holding that under the Supreme Court of Canada's textual, contextual, and purposive statutory interpretation mandate (Canada Trustco, 2005 SCC 54), the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria—repeatedly affirmed by the FCA in RIS-Christie (1998), C.W. Agencies (2001), Jentel (2011), and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. Canada (2016 FCA 152)—are binding law.
8.3 System Uncertainty, Post-Commercial Release R&D, and Expert Witness Rules: 6379249 Canada, Formadrain, National R&D, and Buhler Versatile

In 6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 77), the appellant developed a world-record miniature self-contained wireless portable printer (1.5" × 1.5" × 10") and released 200 commercial units at the end of 2008. When over 20% of customers complained of curled paper output and battery depletion after 5–10 pages instead of 20, the company recalled the product and reopened its SR&ED project in 2009–2010 to investigate slip-clutch felt degradation and static vs. dynamic friction regimes. The CRA denied the 2009–2010 claims, arguing that commercial release in 2008 proved technological uncertainty had ended. Justice D'Auray allowed the appeal in full with costs, establishing that premature commercial release does not bar subsequent work from qualifying as SR&ED, that technological uncertainty "exists in the mind of the specialist" and must be evaluated holistically at the integrated system level, and that the CEO's credible oral testimony established on a balance of probabilities that the 2010 technical report was filed on time under subsection 37(11).

Similarly, in Formadrain Inc. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 42) (involving trenchless underground pipe rehabilitation technologies), Les Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313), and Buhler Versatile Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC 18) (tractor subsystem integration), the Tax Court reinforced that cross-disciplinary engineering projects must be analyzed as an integrated whole rather than dissected into isolated steps, and that highly credible oral testimony from the hands-on inventors can supplement gaps in written documentation.

Conversely, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2020 TCC 47; aff'd 2022 FCA 72), an SR&ED consulting firm claimed credits for developing a web-based Project Tracking System using Classic ASP, COM+, and Microsoft SQL Server 2000, arguing that its self-imposed cost constraint (refusing to purchase SQL Server 2005) and staff familiarity constraints created technological uncertainty. Both the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the claim, holding that self-imposed business or budget constraints using legacy tools do not create objective technological uncertainty, that time-tracking logs and code snippets without documented hypothesis testing fail the scientific method test, and that litigant or expert reports that fail to comply with Section 145(2) of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) and the Code of Conduct for Experts are inadmissible.
8.4 Modern Software, Food Science, Energy, and Penalties Jurisprudence (2023–2026)

In Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC), a food manufacturer appealed the CRA's denial of seven SR&ED projects (2013–2016, totalling $343,449 in expenditures and $60,963 in ITCs across the disclosed years) involving the development of frozen pie recipes designed to extend shelf life without preservatives. The Tax Court ruled in favour of the taxpayer, holding that the company's systematic trials, documented test batches, and forthright CEO testimony satisfied all five Northwest Hydraulic criteria, and noting that the Minister never addressed the detailed technical documentation produced by the business.

In DAZZM Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 129), the taxpayer developed a cloud-based SaaS platform and encountered severe performance bottlenecks when integrating open-source tools (React and Redux). Allowing the appeal, Justice Gagnon confirmed two vital principles for software SR&ED claims: first, that uncertainty arising from the interactions between known open-source components can satisfy "system uncertainty" beyond routine debugging or optimization; and second, at paragraph 119, that "although the CRA would have liked to see contemporaneous time sheets for the work performed, they are not necessarily required for work to be eligible as qualifying SR&ED" where metrics and testimony substantiate the claim.

In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 TCC 159, Amended Reasons Jan 17, 2025), the Toronto food and beverage company claimed SR&ED for its 2020 taxation year for developing Chrisoda, a canned, vinegar-based beverage containing cold-pressed juice that was shelf-stable at room temperature for two years. Cold-pressed juice contained natural microbes that fermented and caused cans to explode, while common preservatives (potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate) caused an undesirable taste and milky appearance. The claimant hypothesized and systematically tested Chiber (a natural mushroom extract that had previously been used only in dairy products and never in juice beverages), measuring microbial counts and pH levels across trials. Justice Bodie allowed the appeal in full, holding that applying a publicly available solution in a novel context where it has never been used establishes genuine technological uncertainty, and that contemporaneous records need not be written for someone unfamiliar with the field to replicate the results.

By contrast, in Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63) (mobile direct-contact frac water heaters), Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 183) (13 food processing projects from 2005–2009), and Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC) (roller-compacted concrete field adjustments), the Tax Court dismissed all three appeals because the work consisted of trial-and-error prototyping with vague hypotheses, reconstructed narratives, and arbitrary wage estimates. In Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173), the Tax Court allowed documented 2007–2008 industrial heating element projects, but denied the 2006 and 2009 claims and held that plagiarized supplier/website text in technical reports constituted a misrepresentation that reopened statute-barred years and supported penalties. Finally, in Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King (2026 TCC 7), the Tax Court issued a split decision on industrial control systems: allowing the MTCLM SIL 4 train-control project due to cumulative "system uncertainty", while disallowing $1,293,692 for the SCADACOM-5 project because modernizing and scaling up an existing system using known tools is product development rather than experimental development.

Overturned CRA denial of 7 food formulation projects where contemporaneous test logs and credible CEO testimony proved all 5 criteria.
Confirmed that "system uncertainty" in integrating open-source software tools qualifies, and contemporaneous timesheets are not strictly mandatory.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 159 / Jan 2025)
Applying a known preservative (Chiber mushroom extract) in a novel domain (cold-pressed juice vs. dairy) establishes technological uncertainty.
Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63)
Denied claim where work was trial-and-error prototyping with vague hypotheses and lacked verifiable systematic testing records.
Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173)
Allowed documented 2007–08 R&D; upheld statute-barred reassessments & s. 163(2) penalties where narratives plagiarized supplier websites.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King (2026 TCC 7)
Allowed SIL 4 train control project on cumulative "system uncertainty"; disallowed $1.29M SCADA modernization/scale-up with known tools.

body.text: 9. Audit Readiness and Strategic Compliance Checklist for Canadian Claimants

To maximize recovery under the expanded 2026 federal and provincial R&D tax architecture while insulating claims against CRA technical and financial audit adjustments, Canadian enterprises and their tax advisors should execute the following seven-point compliance protocol:

items: Re-Model Corporate Group Eligibility Under Bill C-15 ($6M Limit, ECPCs, and Revenue Election): Review all taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, to capture the doubled $6 million enhanced 35% expenditure limit. If the claimant is a Canadian-resident public company (or subsidiary), evaluate qualification as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC). If the claimant is a CCPC whose prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15 million due to debt or equity financing, model the annual election under subsection 127(10.31) to compute the expenditure limit phase-out using three-year average gross revenue ($15M–$75M) rather than taxable capital.

Capture Restored Capital Equipment (ASA ≥90% and SUE >50%) and Lease Costs: Audit all fixed asset additions, lab equipment, 3D printers, testing rigs, computer workstations, and engineering software licences acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024. Implement contemporaneous equipment operating-time logs to substantiate either ≥90% ASA treatment (Line 390, removing the asset from Schedule T2SCH8 CCA) or >50% to <90% First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) treatment (Line 504, claiming 25% of capital cost per term while retaining Schedule T2SCH8 CCA).

Evaluate the Optional CRA Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322): For businesses with gross business income under $25 million launching high-value or technically complex R&D initiatives, consider submitting Form T1322 via My Business Account prior to commencing work to secure an upfront 8-week eligibility determination and lock in the 90-day post-filing refund processing standard.

Optimize Founder Compensation and Respect the 180-Day Rule: Ensure shareholder-employees (specified employees owning ≥10% of any share class) are paid via regular T4 base salary rather than ineligible dividends or excluded bonuses/profit-based remuneration, taking into account the 75% time cap and the 2.5 × YMPE ($186,500 in 2026) Proxy Salary Base ceiling. Verify that all accrued SR&ED wages and non-wage current expenses are physically paid within 180 days of taxation year-end under subsection 78(4) and subsection 127(26).

Embed Contemporaneous Scientific Record-Keeping into Engineering Workflows: As underscored by the Tax Court in DAZZM (2024 TCC 129), Manning Canning (2024 TCC 159), Vortex Energy (2025 TCC 63), and Willowglen Systems (2026 TCC 7), claims succeed or fail on dated, contemporaneous evidence showing iteration and hypothesis testing—such as versioned design documents, benchmark logs, failed prototype data, and lab notebooks showing why standard engineering failed—rather than ex-post reconstructions or copied vendor descriptions.

Structure Customer and Subcontractor Contracts Carefully: Draft customer agreements as fixed-price commercial deliverables where the claimant retains IP and assumes technical and financial risk (preserving ITCs under Com Dev), and ensure arm's length Canadian subcontractors are taxable suppliers whose statements of work explicitly document SR&ED performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf.

Coordinate Provincial Stacking (Québec CRIC, Ontario OITC/ORDTC Waiver, BC Alignment, Alberta IEG): In Québec, transition all claims for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, to Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (CRIC), capturing newly eligible pre-commercialization regulatory testing, product design, and capital equipment. In Ontario, evaluate whether to waive the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC to prevent grinding down the 35% cash-refundable federal ITC in loss years. Finally, calendar the absolute 18-month statutory filing deadline (and 21-month Alberta AT1 Schedule 29 deadline) to ensure all prescribed federal and provincial schedules are filed with zero omissions.
